analysis.title: AI Unwinds: Hedge Funds Just Dumped AI Stocks At The 2nd Fastest Pace In A Year As Net Leverage Tumbles
key_insights: Hedge funds net sold Global AI stocks (GSXGGLAI constituents) for five consecutive sessions, Oct 8-14. All cumulative net buying in the group since the start of 2025 has been reversed, per GS Prime (Vincent Lin).
Oct 14 was the second largest net selling day for Global AI stocks in the past year, behind only July. Long sales outpaced short sales 3.5 to 1, so it was mostly long liquidation.
Oct 14 was the first -1% SPX / -2% NDX session since late July, following a CPI-driven selloff.

Net allocation to Global AI stocks is 26.1% of global single-stock net market value, down from a 31.7% peak in early June. That is the 49th percentile over one year and the 83rd percentile over three years.

The aggregate AI long/short ratio fell to 3.27 from 4.34 at the June peak. That is the 7th percentile over one year and the 64th percentile over three years. Allocation is down about 5.6 points (about a sixth) and the ratio about a quarter from the peak.
AI net exposure is still above any level before 2026 and roughly triple early-2023 levels. One-year percentiles read washed out, three-year percentiles read still long.

JPMorgan's Market Intelligence desk puts its TPM positioning gauge at about the 46th percentile (neutral), versus about the 19th near the late-July lows. It sees room for further de-grossing into key tech catalysts but remains constructive and sees a possible dip-buying opportunity.
GS Asia (Rachel Hu) said Taiwan market color suggested limited capitulation versus the July selloff.

Global equities were significantly net sold on the GS Prime book on Oct 14, a -2.1 standard deviation move over one year, with long sales roughly 3 to 1 over short sales. North America and EM Asia led, with Korea and Taiwan the most net sold markets.

The US made up 66% of global net selling (-1.8 SD), with long to short sales at 1.9 to 1 and single stocks vs macro products (ETFs and futures) split 54%/46%. Eight of 11 US sectors were net sold, led by Info Tech and Industrials, and every Info Tech subsector was net sold.

Hedge funds bought Health Care and Consumer Staples, which GS reads as an incrementally defensive posture. The rotation continued Oct 15 per Reuters, with both sectors up more than 2% in early trading.

Per the article, Korea and Taiwan saw significant net foreign selling overnight on Oct 15, with a record ~$9.3B foreign outflow from Taiwan and circuit breakers in Seoul. The article says the Kospi is down exactly 20% (bear market) a week after a warning that the only buyer had left.
TMT-focused L/S funds lost 2.7% on Oct 14 (-2.6 SD per GS London) and are down 4.5% in October, with YTD gains cut to 13.1%.

Global fundamental L/S funds lost 0.9% on the day, mainly on beta losses, and are down 2.1% MTD (+10.5% YTD). Asia-focused L/S funds lost 0.9%, are down 4.1% MTD and are up 19.3% YTD versus a +40% peak in late June.
Global systematic L/S funds gained 0.5% on the day, 1.9% MTD and 21.7% YTD, the best of the groups.

GS prime book gross leverage fell 0.4 points to 310.3% (up 0.6 points MTD), in the 72nd, 91st and 94th percentiles on one, three and five-year lookbacks. Net leverage fell 1.5 points to 73.3% (down 4.3 points MTD), the 6th percentile over one year, 22nd over three and 42nd over five.

The Zerohedge author argues high gross with low net leaves funds with more to sell than net exposure suggests, and de-grossing becomes the only exit when crowded longs and crowded shorts move against them together, as in late July.

GS Delta-One (Rich Privorotsky): the bank's global neocloud basket fell 20% in five sessions, about a 1st percentile move over ten years. The desk said the pain trade was long AI / short bonds and both sides are now unwinding.

The 10Y yield fell to a three-week low around 5.07%. The article links this to AI no longer crowding out duration and cites BofA's OpenAI 'tell' note scenario of AI stocks and yields falling together.

Per Reuters cited in the article, the Nasdaq hit a near one-month low, CoreWeave fell another 8.5% after Wednesday's drop, and the SOX was tracking a seventh straight loss and about $2T of lost market cap.

The author leans bearish: with AI net exposure in the 83rd percentile over three years, gross leverage in the 94th percentile over five years and record foreign selling in Asia, the unwind looks closer to its beginning than its end. JPM takes the buy-the-dip view.

market_movers.rationale: CoreWeave fell another 8.5% on Oct 15 after Wednesday's drop, per Reuters cited in the article. Part of a neocloud basket down 20% in five sessions.

sector_views.rationale: Hedge funds net sold Info Tech and Industrials most on Oct 14, and every Info Tech subsector (software, semis, IT services) was net sold.
Hedge funds bought Health Care and Consumer Staples, which GS reads as an incrementally defensive posture. Both sectors were up more than 2% in early trading on Oct 15.
Hedge funds bought staples on Oct 14, and the sector was up more than 2% in early trading on Oct 15.

earnings_insights: Per the article, Anthropic's $16.8 billion quarter did not stop the AI selloff. The basis (revenue vs other) is not stated.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Three-week low. The article reads it as AI no longer crowding out duration, with stocks and yields falling together.
Down 0.4 points on the day, up 0.6 points MTD, near five-year highs (94th percentile). A large gross book raises de-grossing risk.
Down 1.5 points on the day and 4.3 points MTD, 6th percentile over one year. Low directional conviction.

risk_factors: Further de-grossing from a gross book near five-year highs if crowded longs and shorts move against funds together.
AI exposure still elevated on three-year percentiles (83rd for allocation, 64th for long/short ratio), leaving room for more selling.
Record foreign selling in Korea and Taiwan, with a Kospi bear market and circuit breakers in Seoul.
Financing constraints on AI compute buildout, per Privorotsky: compute demand can grow exponentially but the capital to finance it cannot.
A potential AI debt bubble unwind, with BofA's scenario of stocks and yields falling together.
Limited capitulation in Taiwan per GS Asia, suggesting more selling to come.
charts_described: GS chart of hedge fund flows in AI names since the start of 2025: net flow (black) fell back to the zero line, short flow (red) sits near its period lows at about -13% of starting gross MV, and long flow (blue) has rolled over since a Feb-March peak near +30%.

GS Prime chart of net allocation to Global AI stocks as a share of global single-stock net market value, 26.1% against a 31.7% early-June peak. The text says AI net exposure is higher than at any point before 2026 and roughly triple early 2023.
vol_and_positioning: GS Prime: Global AI stocks saw their second largest net selling in a year on Oct 14, with long sales outpacing short sales 3.5 to 1.

Cumulative hedge fund net flow into AI names since Jan 2025 is back to zero. Short flow sits near its period lows at about -13% of starting gross market value, and long flow has been rolling over since a Feb-March peak near +30%.
AI net allocation is 26.1% of global single-stock net market value (peak 31.7% in early June). The long/short ratio is 3.27 (peak 4.34).
Net exposure to Mag7 as a share of total US exposure on the GS prime book was near 22% the prior week, the highest on record.
Prime book gross leverage is 310.3% (94th percentile over five years) and net leverage 73.3% (6th percentile over one year).
JPM's TPM positioning gauge is at about the 46th percentile versus about the 19th near the late-July lows.
The late-July event was the largest 3-day de-gross on GS Prime records since Nov '22.
Net leverage among US fundamental L/S funds had earlier fallen to 'Liberation Day' lows, and hedge funds had sold Info Tech at the fastest pace in seven weeks.
cross_bank_references: JPMorgan Market Intelligence: 'we remain constructive on the sector and still see a possible opportunity to buy the dip', while also seeing room for further de-grossing.
Goldman's flow desk saw the technical tide turning for year-end two days earlier, which the author says may no longer hold.
BofA's OpenAI 'tell' note laid out the scenario of the AI bubble bursting with stocks and yields tumbling.

tension_points.bull_case: JPM stays constructive and sees a possible dip-buying opportunity. The JPM positioning gauge is neutral at about the 46th percentile, and GS's flow desk saw the technical tide turning for year-end. One-year percentiles show positioning as washed out (AI net allocation 49th percentile, long/short ratio 7th percentile).
tension_points.bear_case: Three-year percentiles remain elevated (allocation 83rd, long/short ratio 64th), gross leverage is in the 94th percentile over five years, and Taiwan showed limited capitulation. The author sees the unwind nearer its beginning than its end, and JPM itself flags room for further de-grossing into tech catalysts.
